intro: Every law described in this annex was drawn from public summaries of each state's election statutes, chiefly the compendium maintained by Ballotpedia, and from federal election rules. It is included so that no reader can say the door was hidden. The numbers matter less than the lesson they teach: in most of America, the barrier to a new party is not money and it is not popularity. It is paperwork, patience, and signatures. A motivated precinct can clear these hurdles. Most never try.

Read your state's entry, then verify it. Election laws change, secretaries of state reissue handbooks, and deadlines shift with every legislative session. Your county election office will usually hand you the current forms for the asking, free. This annex is a map of the terrain as it stood when the book was compiled. It is orientation, not legal advice.

One federal note before the states. At the national level, a political party committee must register with the Federal Election Commission once it accepts contributions or makes expenditures above $1,000 in a calendar year, and the law gives it only ten days after crossing that line to file. That is the whole federal threshold. There is no wealth test to found a party in America. There is only a form, a filing cabinet, and people willing to sign their names.
The states follow in alphabetical order. Each entry covers three things: how a new party gets on the ballot, how its candidates qualify, and what the party must do to keep its place.

states.Alabama:
A group becomes a full political party in Alabama only when its candidate for a state office draws more than 20 percent of the vote in a general election. Everyone else starts as a minor party. The path: submit the party emblem to the Secretary of State at least 60 days before the primary, then file a certificate of nomination by 5 p.m. on primary day. For statewide ballot access, the party must file a petition signed by at least 3 percent of the total vote cast for governor in the last general election. Minor parties are not required to give notice of the meeting where they nominate candidates.
Sources: https://www.sos.alabama.gov/alabama-votes (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Alabama. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Alaska:
Alaska sorts newcomers into two boxes. A political group files a simple application with the director of the Division of Elections, and the state starts tracking how many voters register under its name. A recognized political party needs at least 5,000 registered voters. To convert, a group must file its application and bylaws with the director of elections, and with the U.S. Department of Justice, on or before May 31 of the election year. There is also a limited political party track for presidential races only: file a petition, and the status holds if the party's presidential candidate wins at least 3 percent of the vote.
Sources: https://www.elections.alaska.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Alaska. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Arizona:
A new party files a petition with the Secretary of State carrying signatures equal to at least 1.33 percent of the total votes cast for governor at the last general election. Signatures must come from at least five counties, and at least 10 percent of them must come from counties with populations under 500,000. The petition is due at least 250 days before the primary. Recognition runs through the next two general elections. After that, the party must poll 5 percent in the governor's race, or hold the affiliation of 0.67 percent of all registered voters by October 1 of the year before the election, or start over.
Sources: https://azsos.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Arizona. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Arkansas:
The petition to the Secretary of State needs 10,000 signatures from registered voters, filed at least three weeks before the primary. Signatures cannot be gathered before January 1 of the year following the last general election. Once the petition is certified, the new party nominates its first slate of candidates by convention. If its candidate for governor or for presidential elector pulls at least 3 percent of the vote at that general election, the party keeps its status and may nominate by primary from then on. Miss the 3 percent mark, and the party ceases to exist as a legal party.
Sources: https://www.sos.arkansas.gov/elections (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Arkansas. Rules change; call before you file.
states.California:
Three doors. A party qualifies if its candidates polled at least 2 percent of the statewide vote at the last gubernatorial primary, or if voters equal to 0.33 percent of registered voters declare for the party by the 154th day before the primary, or if a petition is filed bearing signatures from 10 percent of the voters who cast ballots in the last gubernatorial election. The petition route runs through county election officials, with the Secretary of State ruling by the 135th day before the primary. To stay qualified, a party needs 2 percent in a statewide race or 0.33 percent registration. Fall below 0.067 percent and the ballot line is gone.
Sources: https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_California. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Colorado:
Colorado offers a starter rung called the qualified political organization. File a proof of organization form with bylaws and leadership, meet at least once a year, elect officers in odd-numbered years, pick candidates in even years, and certify at least one candidate every two years. From there, minor party status comes three ways: a statewide candidate takes 5 percent in either of the last two elections; 1,000 registered voters affiliate by July 1; or a petition of 10,000 signatures reaches the Secretary of State by the second Friday of January. Keep status with 1 percent in either of the last two elections, or 1,000 registered affiliates by July 1.
Sources: https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/elections/main.html (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Colorado. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Connecticut:
There is no paperwork phase. A group runs a candidate with a party designation on a nominating petition, and if that candidate wins 1 percent of the vote for the office, a minor party is born, for that office. Hold the status by filing party rules with the Secretary of State, by running a candidate every time the office comes up, and by observing the convention rules: rules on file 60 days before delegates are chosen, written notice to the Secretary of State five days before any nominating convention, and a notice published in a newspaper of general circulation. Major party status requires 20 percent for governor, or 20 percent of registered voters enrolled.
Sources: https://portal.ct.gov/sots/election-services (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Connecticut. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Delaware:
Delaware's gate is registration, not petition. A party appears on the general election ballot only if voters affiliated with it, as of 21 days before the primary, equal at least 0.1 percent of all registered voters in the state, counted against the December 31 roster from the year before the election. To count as a major party, that affiliation must reach 5 percent of the state's registered voters by December 31 before a general election year. Everyone else is a minor party. The practical work here is signing people up as registered members, neighbor by neighbor, county by county.
Sources: https://elections.delaware.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Delaware. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Florida:
A group becomes a minor party by filing a certificate with the Division of Elections: the party name, its officers and executive committee members with a completed uniform voter registration application for each showing their affiliation, and a copy of its constitution, bylaws, and rules. The executive committee then elects a chair, vice chair, secretary, and treasurer. That is the whole doorway. If 5 percent of the state's registered voters sign up by January 1 before a primary, the party is reclassified as a major party. In the primary, multiple candidates of the party face only its own registered members; a single candidate skips straight to the general ballot.
Sources: https://dos.fl.gov/elections/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Florida. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Georgia:
Georgia calls most new groups political organizations. Register with the Secretary of State within 60 days of forming, with a $10 filing fee, a charter, bylaws, and officer lists; amendments cost $2 and are due within 30 days of a change. To nominate candidates by convention, the organization either files a petition signed by voters equal to 1 percent of the registered voters from the preceding general election, or points to a statewide nominee from the last election who drew votes equal to 1 percent of registered voters. Without one of those, its candidates are nominated by petition, exactly as independent candidates are. Full party status requires 20 percent for governor or president.
Sources: https://mvp.sos.ga.gov/s/olvr-home (Georgia voter-registration portal); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Georgia. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Hawaii:
Apply to the Office of Elections, which issues the official petition. The signature bar is small: 0.1 percent of the state's registered voters as of the most recent general election. File by the 170th day before the primary, together with the names and addresses of the party's central committee and county committee officers, and a copy of the party rules. A party that qualifies by petition and keeps qualifying for three consecutive elections earns ten years of automatic ballot access, provided it keeps fielding candidates. When the ten years run out, it must hit the vote thresholds again or re-petition.
Sources: https://elections.hawaii.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Hawaii. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Idaho:
Three doors. Run three or more candidates under the party name at a general election. Or poll 3 percent of the vote for governor or presidential electors. Or file a petition with the Secretary of State by August 30 of an even-numbered year, signed by electors equal to 2 percent of the vote for presidential electors at the last presidential election. The petition states the party's name in six words or fewer and may not be circulated before August 30 of the year before the election. Once the Secretary of State certifies the petition, the party holds a state convention and nominates like any other party.
Sources: https://vote.idaho.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Idaho. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Illinois:
The new party petition is the door. Statewide, the requirement is the lesser of 1 percent of the voters who cast ballots at the last general election, or 25,000 signatures. For a congressional or legislative district, it is 5 percent of that district's last general election turnout, or the statewide number, whichever is less. Petitions may be circulated no more than 90 days before the filing deadline. The old full-slate rule, which forced new parties to run a candidate for every office at once, was struck down by the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals in 2017. A party becomes established when its candidate for governor takes 5 percent, and only established parties run primaries.
Sources: https://www.elections.il.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Illinois. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Indiana:
Indiana measures everything against the Secretary of State's race. A party whose candidate finished first or second there is a major party. One that took between 2 and 10 percent may nominate by state, county, or municipal convention. Before recognition, a new party's candidates file by petition, exactly as independents do, except the petition may carry the party's name and device. Take 2 percent for Secretary of State and the party earns the convention route from then on. Reach 10 percent, and it must nominate by primary election, which in Indiana is the mark of arrival.
Sources: https://www.in.gov/sos/elections/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Indiana. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Iowa:
A group that is not a party files nothing to exist. It is a nonparty political organization, and each one may nominate a single candidate per partisan office using nomination papers: an affidavit of candidacy plus nomination petitions or a certificate from an organization convention. To become a party, put a candidate for president or governor on the general ballot, win at least 2 percent of the vote for that office, then file an application for party status with the Secretary of State after the canvass, within one year of the election. Hold on by clearing 2 percent at every general election. Fall short, and the status is revoked and the climb begins again.
Sources: https://sos.iowa.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Iowa. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Kansas:
Petition the Secretary of State with signatures from qualified electors equal to 2 percent of the total vote for governor at the last general election, filed by noon on June 1 before the primary. The name cannot be so long, or so close to an existing party's name, that voters would be confused. Parties whose candidate for governor took 5 percent must nominate by primary. Everyone else nominates at a state convention and files a certified nominee list with the Secretary of State by noon on June 1 of the election year. To keep recognition, a party needs a statewide candidate who wins at least 1 percent of the vote.
Sources: https://www.sos.ks.gov/elections/elections.html (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Kansas. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Kentucky:
Kentucky requires no paperwork at all to form a party. The state classifies political entities purely by their results in the most recent presidential election. A candidate who took at least 10 percent makes the entity a political party, which nominates by primary. Between 2 and 10 percent makes it a political organization, which may nominate by convention, by primary, or by petition. Below 2 percent is a political group, and a political group's only route to the ballot is the nominating petition. The message is blunt: the party name arrives as a reward for votes already earned.
Sources: https://elect.ky.gov/Pages/default.aspx (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Kentucky. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Louisiana:
Two doors. The registration door: 5,000 registered voters affiliated with the party, a notarized registration statement, and a $5,000 fee, all delivered to the Secretary of State no later than 90 days before the candidate qualifying period opens. The results door: a candidate who took 5 percent in the last presidential election, or 5 percent in a statewide primary or general election. Keep recognition by staying on the ballot; four consecutive years without a qualified primary candidate ends it. One warning for this project: as of August 1, 2025, Louisiana will not recognize any party whose name is simply Independent or any variation on it.
Sources: https://voterportal.sos.la.gov/ (Louisiana voter portal); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Louisiana. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Maine:
Two roads. Around a candidate: file a declaration naming a governor or presidential candidate from the last election who was nominated by petition and won at least 5 percent, with that candidate's signed consent, by 5 p.m. on the 180th day before the primary. By enrollment: ten or more voters file a declaration between December 1 and December 30 of an even-numbered year, then gather 5,000 enrolled members by January 2 of the following year. A new party must hold municipal caucuses in the state's 16 counties and a state convention. Keep status with 5 percent for governor or president, or 5,000 enrolled members.
Sources: https://www.maine.gov/sos/cec/elec/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Maine. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Maryland:
File a formation petition naming the party, its chairman, and the 25 registered voters who will form the initial governing body, along with an interim constitution and bylaws. Supporters then have the two years between the first signature and the last to collect 10,000 signatures from eligible voters. Within 90 days of filing, the chairman convenes an organizational meeting to adopt the constitution and bylaws; a copy goes to the state board within 30 days of adoption. Status lasts through the second statewide general election after qualification. After that, keep it by winning 1 percent for the highest office on the ballot, or by holding 1 percent of registered voters as of December 31 each year.
Sources: https://elections.maryland.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Maryland. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Massachusetts:
A party is any organization that polled 3 percent of the vote for a statewide office at the last statewide election, or that has enrolled 1 percent of the state's registered voters. There is a lighter option called the political designation: up to three words, requested by at least 50 registered voters on a form to the secretary of the commonwealth. Voters enrolled in a designation may still vote in party primaries. The upkeep rule mirrors the entry rule: miss both the 3 percent mark and the 1 percent enrollment mark, and the party ceases to be recognized.
Sources: https://www.usvotefoundation.org/vote/state-election-offices.htm (US Vote Foundation election-office directory); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Massachusetts. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Michigan:
Petition the Secretary of State with signatures equal to 1 percent of all votes cast for governor at the most recent gubernatorial election, including at least 100 signatures from each of at least one half of the state's congressional districts. A certificate signed by the party's chairperson and secretary must reach the Secretary of State by 4 p.m. on the 110th day before the general election. Signatures must be no more than 180 days old when filed, and a sufficiency decision comes no later than 60 days before the election. To keep status, the party's best-performing candidate must win at least 1 percent of the votes cast for the winning Secretary of State candidate.
Sources: https://www.michigan.gov/sos/elections (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Michigan. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Minnesota:
Two classes, two ladders. A major party needs a statewide candidate whose votes, cast in every county, total at least 8 percent of all votes cast in the election, or a full slate of 76 candidates, or a petition signed by 5 percent of the voters of the preceding general election collected within one year. A minor party needs the same at 1 percent. Status lasts through two consecutive general elections; keep it by hitting the numbers again within those two. A district-level minor party needs 10 percent there. Minor parties nominate by petition rather than primary, and must certify a constitution, a chair, and a convention to the Secretary of State by December 31.
Sources: https://www.sos.state.mn.us/elections-voting/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Minnesota. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Mississippi:
The gentlest entry in the country. No petitions, no fees, and no vote minimums to keep recognition. The chairman of the party's state executive committee files a registration application with the Secretary of State within 30 days of the party's organization, accompanied by an affidavit listing the members of the executive committee, its chairman and secretary, the national committeeman and committeewoman, and the party's officers. The only real restriction is the name: it cannot match, or be deceptively similar to, any political body already registered. Organize, file, and the party exists in the eyes of the state.
Sources: https://www.ms.gov/ (Mississippi state government homepage); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Mississippi. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Missouri:
Petition the Secretary of State. Statewide, the petition needs 10,000 registered voters. For a single district, the requirement is the lesser of 2 percent of the votes cast at the last election for the office sought, or 10,000. Each page must declare the intent to form a new party and give the party's name in five words or fewer. The window opens at 8 a.m. the day after one general election and closes at 5 p.m. on the 15th Monday before the general the party wants to enter. The first slate is nominated however the bylaws prescribe; after that, nominations go through the primary. Keep status with more than 2 percent in either of the last two elections.
Sources: https://www.sos.mo.gov/elections (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Missouri. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Montana:
The petition must carry signatures equal to 5 percent of the votes cast for the winning gubernatorial candidate, or 5,000 electors, whichever is less, and must include voters from at least one third of the state's legislative districts, with at least 5 percent, or 150 electors, in each of those districts. Four weeks before the filing deadline, the petition and circulation affidavits go to the county election administrator where the signatures were gathered for verification; the administrator forwards them to the Secretary of State at least 95 days before the primary. A party whose statewide candidate drew 5 percent in either of the last two elections nominates by primary.
Sources: https://sosmt.gov/Elections/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Montana. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Nebraska:
File a sample petition with the Secretary of State before circulating anything. The finished petition needs signatures equal to 1 percent of the vote for governor at the most recent election, spread so that each of the three congressional districts supplies at least 1 percent. The deadline is January 15 to enter the primary, July 15 for the general. The Secretary of State rules on sufficiency within 20 business days, and a certified party then has 20 days to file its constitution, bylaws, and a list of officers. Keep access by holding 10,000 registered affiliates, or by a 5 percent statewide showing, or a combination of district races adding up to 5 percent, in one of the last two elections.
Sources: https://sos.nebraska.gov/elections (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Nebraska. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Nevada:
File a certificate of existence with the Secretary of State, along with the party's constitution or bylaws, which must provide a nomination procedure allowing one candidate per office. Then prove support: signatures equal to 1 percent of the votes cast for U.S. Representative at the last general election, apportioned equally among the state's four districts, filed by June 1. Alternatives: a party candidate already won 1 percent at the last election, or 1 percent of registered voters declared for the party by January 1. A notarized candidate list goes in during the filing period, or a notice of continued existence by the second Friday in August. Keep status with 1 percent of the vote or 1 percent registration.
Sources: https://www.nvsos.gov/sos/elections (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Nevada. Rules change; call before you file.
states.New Hampshire:
Recognition belongs to any political organization whose candidate won at least 4 percent of the vote for governor or United States Senator at the last state general election. Everyone else petitions: valid signatures equal to 3 percent of the total votes cast at the previous state general election, with no one signing more than one organization's paper. The chairman files a declaration of intent during the June filing period, and petition papers land by 5 p.m. on the Wednesday one week before the primary. Recognized parties nominate by primary. Between the third Tuesday of September and the last Tuesday of October, the party holds a state convention to adopt a platform and set its organization.
Sources: https://www.usa.gov/state-election-office (USA.gov election-office directory); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_New_Hampshire. Rules change; call before you file.
states.New Jersey:
The bar is a single number. A party is any organization whose candidates polled at least 10 percent of the total vote cast for the General Assembly at the preceding election. Candidates petition onto the ballot with a designation of three words or fewer, which is printed beside their names. Reach 10 percent, and the party may nominate by primary; keep reaching it, and the status holds. Before that milestone, New Jersey's newcomers run and vote through petition designations, one office and one election at a time, accumulating a name the way a riverbank accumulates silt.
Sources: https://www.nj.gov/state/elections/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_New_Jersey. Rules change; call before you file.
states.New Mexico:
File party rules with the Secretary of State, uniform county rules with the county clerks, and a petition carrying valid signatures equal to 0.5 percent of the vote for governor at the last general election. Everything is due within 30 days of the party's organization, and no later than 23 days after the primary before the election the party intends to enter. Rule amendments are barred within 120 days of a general election and take effect 30 days after filing. A party loses status by skipping two elections in a row, or by a governor or presidential candidate drawing under 0.5 percent. Major status requires 5 percent of the vote plus one third of one percent of the state's registered voters.
Sources: https://www.sos.nm.gov/voting-and-elections/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_New_Mexico. Rules change; call before you file.
states.New York:
There is no advance registration for parties. A political organization runs a candidate for governor or president through the independent nomination process, printing its chosen name on the petition, and the name appears on the ballot beside the candidate. If the candidate wins at least 2 percent of the vote for the office, or 130,000 votes, whichever is greater, the organization is recognized as a party. It then forms state and county committees, files its rules within 10 days of adopting them, nominates by its own rules the first time, and by primary thereafter. Fall below the number, and the party's voters are unenrolled; the climb starts again.
Sources: https://www.ny.gov/services/register-vote (New York voter-registration service); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_New_York. Rules change; call before you file.
states.North Carolina:
Three doors. A candidate for governor or presidential elector polls 2 percent of the statewide vote. Or a petition reaches the State Board of Elections by noon on June 1 with signatures equal to 0.25 percent of the voters who voted for governor, including at least 200 registered voters from each of three congressional districts; petitions go to the county chairman for verification 15 days before the state deadline. Or documentation that the group placed a presidential candidate on the general election ballots of at least 70 percent of the states at the prior presidential election. A newly qualified party selects its first nominees by convention.
Sources: https://www.ncsbe.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_North_Carolina. Rules change; call before you file.
states.North Dakota:
A party may nominate on the primary ballot once it has organized under state law, and its candidates for presidential electors, governor, attorney general, or secretary of state took at least 5 percent of the vote at the last general election. Short of that, a political organization files a petition with the Secretary of State signed by at least 7,000 qualified electors, by 4 p.m. on the 64th day before the primary, naming the organization, stating its platform principles, and listing the candidates it wants on the primary ballot. The 5 percent test is also the upkeep test. Miss it, and the party re-petitions.
Sources: https://vip.sos.nd.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_North_Dakota. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Ohio:
A party exists on two conditions. Its candidate for governor, or its nominees for presidential electors, polled at least 3 percent of the vote at the most recent regular state election, which buys four years of status. Or it files a party formation petition: signatures equal to at least 1 percent of the vote for governor or presidential electors, with at least 500 qualified electors from each of at least half the congressional districts, a declared party name, and a committee of three to five petitioners, filed for an election held more than 125 days after filing. The Secretary of State blocks names likely to confuse voters with an existing party.
Sources: https://www.voteohio.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Ohio. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Oklahoma:
File a notice of intent with the State Election Board, at any time except between March 1 and November 15 of even-numbered years. Then circulate a qualifying petition for up to one year, collecting signatures equal to 3 percent of the vote for governor at the last general election, never gathering between March 1 and November 15 of an even year. File by March 1 of an election year to reach that year's ballot. Recognized parties nominate by primary. Keep status with at least 2.5 percent for any statewide office in either of the last two elections. A party that slips becomes a political organization, and the designation terminates after four years unless the party re-qualifies.
Sources: https://oklahoma.gov/elections.html (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Oklahoma. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Oregon:
File a signed prospective petition with the Secretary of State, then gather signatures equal to 1.5 percent of the votes cast for all candidates for governor at the most recent election at which a governor was elected to a full term. The completed petition is due within two years of that first filing. Keep status one of two ways: registration equal to 0.25 percent of the state's electors, or 0.1 percent registration plus at least one candidate polling 1 percent for presidential elector or a single statewide office once in any four-year period. Minor parties nominate by convention and must file their organizational documents within 30 days of adopting them.
Sources: https://sos.oregon.gov/elections/pages/default.aspx (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Oregon. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Pennsylvania:
Pennsylvania grades on two curves. Party status comes from a candidate who polled at least 2 percent of the largest countywide vote in each of at least ten counties and 2 percent of the largest statewide vote, or 5 percent of the largest countywide vote in any single county at the preceding general or municipal election. Parties whose statewide registration is under 15 percent of the combined registration of all statewide parties are minor parties: no primaries, and candidates qualify through nomination papers bearing a body name of three words or fewer printed on the ballot. The giants hold the primaries. Everyone else petitions.
Sources: https://www.vote.pa.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Pennsylvania. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Rhode Island:
A political organization becomes a party by nominating a candidate for governor or president who wins 5 percent of the vote, or by petition: signatures from registered voters equal to 5 percent of the votes cast for governor or president at the last election, none collected before January 1 of the target year. Petition-qualified status lasts only for that year. File the organization's name, chairperson, and secretary with the board of elections when the petitions go in. The deadline is June 1 for parties nominating by primary, August 1 for any other method. Keep recognition the way it was won: 5 percent for governor or president, or start over.
Sources: https://elections.ri.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Rhode_Island. Rules change; call before you file.
states.South Carolina:
Petition the state election commission for certification at least six months before the election, with 10,000 or more registered electors, and a name substantially different from any previously certified party. Then organize like you mean it: county conventions before March 31 of each general election year, a state convention before May 15 publicly announced at least ten days ahead, and nominations by convention or party primary. The party must certify candidates in at least one of any two consecutive November general elections, or in an election between them. Miss that rhythm and the certification lapses. The state wants to see a living organization, not a name on file.
Sources: https://scvotes.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_South_Carolina. Rules change; call before you file.
states.South Dakota:
A party is any group whose candidate for a statewide office received at least 2.5 percent of the vote in either of the two previous general elections. A new party organizes by filing a petition with the Secretary of State by 5 p.m. on the last Tuesday of March before the primary, signed by registered voters equal to 1 percent of the vote for governor at the last gubernatorial election. The written declaration must carry the party's name and a brief statement of its principles. The party then adopts a constitution or bylaws, filed with any amendments within 30 days of approval, and joins the primary.
Sources: https://sdsos.gov/elections-voting/default.aspx (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_South_Dakota. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Tennessee:
Petition the Coordinator of Elections with signatures equal to 2.5 percent of the vote for governor at the last gubernatorial election, the petition's purpose, the party's name, and signatures of registered voters from a single county. Petitions are issued no more than 90 days before the qualifying deadline. Before any name touches a ballot, the party's officers file two things with the Secretary of State and the coordinator: an affidavit that the party does not advocate overthrow of any government by force, and the party's rules, with amendments filed within 30 days and effective ten days after filing. Keep the ballot with a 5 percent statewide showing, which also brings automatic access.
Sources: https://sos.tn.gov/elections (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Tennessee. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Texas:
Form an organization with a name of three words or fewer, elect a chair, and file party rules with the Secretary of State covering convention procedure, the selection of presidential electors, and the choosing of officers and delegates. A party making state nominations also establishes a state executive committee and posts all its rules on its website. The nominating ladder runs from precinct conventions up through county, district, and state conventions, each chair certifying nominees within 20 days. Ballot access requires precinct convention participants totaling 1 percent of all votes for governor at the last gubernatorial election, made up by petition if short. Keep the ballot with a statewide nominee at 5 percent.
Sources: https://www.votetexas.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Texas. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Utah:
A registered party files a petition with the lieutenant governor signed by at least 2,000 registered voters, stating a party name of no more than four words and an emblem distinguishable from every other party's. Its candidates then reach the primary ballot by gathering petition signatures. Full qualified party status, under the state's signature-and-convention law, lets candidates pursue the nomination through the party's convention system, or by petition, or both. Whichever level a party holds, it keeps it only if one of its candidates wins at least 2 percent of all votes cast for the United States House of Representatives in the same regular general election.
Sources: https://vote.utah.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Utah. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Vermont:
Vermont organizes from the ground up, in odd-numbered years. Three voters in a town call a caucus, noticed at the town clerk's office at least five days ahead, and elect a town committee with a chair, vice chair, secretary, treasurer, and assistant treasurer; certified lists go to the Secretary of State, the state chair, and the town clerk within 72 hours. A minor party may skip the county tier unless it wants to nominate state senate candidates. The state committee certifies its officers, and by January 1 of the election year the party files a certificate showing organization in at least 30 towns. Major parties, at 5 percent, nominate by primary; minors nominate by party committee.
Sources: https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Vermont. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Virginia:
Organize first: a state central committee with one registered voter from each congressional district and two from the commonwealth at large, a party plan, bylaws, and a chairman and secretary in place at least six months before the petition. Then petition: 10,000 qualified voters, including 400 from each congressional district, all signing on or after January 1 of the election year, filed with the state board of elections by noon on the 74th day before the election. Official recognition, and the party label beside statewide candidates, arrives when a party candidate wins at least 10 percent of the vote for a statewide office in either of the last two elections.
Sources: https://www.elections.virginia.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Virginia. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Washington:
The easiest state in the union for a new label. Under the top-two primary, any candidate simply lists the party they prefer, and the law requires no conventions and no signatures, and does not even dictate how a party conducts its nominations. A major political party is one whose nominees for president and vice president took at least 5 percent of the vote at the last presidential election; every other organization is a minor party. The parties decide their own nomination methods for themselves. Ballot fights in Washington are won by filing candidates on time, not by petitioning anyone.
Sources: https://www.sos.wa.gov/elections (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Washington. Rules change; call before you file.
states.West Virginia:
A party is any affiliation of voters whose candidate for governor polled at least 1 percent of the total vote at the last general election. Until then, independents carry the flag: a candidate may choose a political designation of no more than five words and specify it on the nominating petition form. A party, in fact, can only be formed by running a candidate under a party designation and letting the votes accumulate. One percent is the whole law. The gate at the start is light, the gate for keeping is light, and every general election offers a fresh chance to cross.
Sources: https://sos.wv.gov/elections/Pages/default.aspx (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_West_Virginia. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Wisconsin:
Three routes. A candidate for any statewide office took at least 1 percent at the last gubernatorial election, or 1 percent at a general that coincided with a presidential election. An organization that was listed as independent and met that same test asks the Wisconsin Elections Commission for ballot status by 5 p.m. on April 1 of an election year. Or petition with the signatures of at least 10,000 qualified electors, including at least 1,000 from each of three separate congressional districts, also by April 1, for status through that year's general election. Parties with ballot status nominate by primary, and keep it by repeating the 1 percent test each cycle.
Sources: https://elections.wi.gov/ (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Wisconsin. Rules change; call before you file.
states.Wyoming:
File a petition with the Secretary of State by May 1 of the election year, signed by electors equal to 2 percent of the vote for Wyoming's at-large U.S. representative at the last general election, after the Secretary has approved the petition's form. Party names may run two words, must not resemble an existing party's, and cannot include the word independent. The filed party enters the next general election as a provisional party, nominating by convention, with statewide nominees certified to the Secretary of State by the day before the primary, and county nominees to the county clerk. Minor status runs from 2 to 10 percent. Major status, with its own primaries, begins at 10.
Sources: https://sos.wyo.gov/Elections/Default.aspx (state election office); Ballotpedia: https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_access_requirements_for_political_parties_in_Wyoming. Rules change; call before you file.

closing: Fifty states, fifty doors, and not one of them asks whether a party is liberal or conservative. They ask whether it can organize a meeting, gather signatures, and show up on time. That is the entire secret the ballot laws keep. The duopoly is not protected by money alone. It is protected by the assumption, repeated until it feels like physics, that none of us will ever do the paperwork.
